enonce_markdown: A cyclist and her bicycle have a combined mass of $80\,\mathrm{kg}$ and travel along a straight road at $5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Their momentum is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Linear momentum is the product of mass and velocity: $p = mv$, in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

### Solution

$p = mv = 80 \times 5 = 400\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

$16$ is $m/v$; $85$ adds mass and speed; $200$ wrongly uses $\tfrac{1}{2}mv$ (a mix-up with kinetic energy). **Answer: d.**

enonce_markdown: Two children wearing roller skates stand together, at rest, on smooth level tiles. They push against each other's hands and move apart in opposite directions. Friction is negligible. Immediately after the push, the total momentum of the two children is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Principle of conservation of linear momentum: if no external resultant force acts on a system, its total momentum stays constant. Momentum is a vector, so momenta in opposite directions cancel.

### Solution

Before the push the children are at rest, so the total momentum is zero. No external horizontal force acts (friction is negligible), so the total momentum after the push is still zero.

The heavier child moves off more slowly and the lighter child faster, so that the two momenta are equal in size and opposite in direction and cancel. Adding the sizes of the momenta (option d) forgets that momentum is a vector. **Answer: c.**

choix.texte: Twice the momentum of the lighter child.
The momentum of the heavier child only.
Zero, because the two momenta are equal in size and opposite in direction.
The sum of the sizes of their momenta, because both children gain momentum.

enonce_markdown: A railway wagon of mass $6\,000\,\mathrm{kg}$ rolls at $2.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ towards a stationary wagon of mass $2\,000\,\mathrm{kg}$ on a level track. They couple together and move off as one. Their speed just after coupling is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In a collision where the bodies stick together, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after: $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = (m_1 + m_2)v$.

### Solution

Before: $6\,000 \times 2.0 + 2\,000 \times 0 = 12\,000\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

After: $(6\,000 + 2\,000)\,v = 8\,000\,v$.

$8\,000\,v = 12\,000 \Rightarrow v = 1.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

$1.0$ is the average of the two speeds; $2.0$ supposes that the speed does not change; $6.0$ divides by the mass of the stationary wagon only. **Answer: b.**

enonce_markdown: A rifle of mass $4\,\mathrm{kg}$, held loosely and initially at rest, recoils with a speed of $1.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ when it fires a bullet of mass $15\,\mathrm{g}$. Ignoring the mass of the gases, the speed of the bullet is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The total momentum is zero before firing, so it is zero afterwards: the momentum of the bullet and the momentum of the rifle are equal in size and opposite in direction, $m_b v_b = M V$. All masses must be in kilograms.

### Solution

$m_b = 15\,\mathrm{g} = 0.015\,\mathrm{kg}$.

$0.015\,v_b = 4 \times 1.5 = 6 \Rightarrow v_b = \dfrac{6}{0.015} = 400\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

$0.0225$ multiplies the bullet mass by the recoil speed; $0.4$ uses $15$ without converting grams to kilograms; $6$ is the momentum, not yet divided by the mass of the bullet. **Answer: d.**

enonce_markdown:
Two trolleys run towards each other along a straight, level, frictionless track. Trolley P has mass $3\,\mathrm{kg}$ and moves to the right at $4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Trolley Q has mass $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ and moves to the left at $3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. They collide and stick together.

(i) Taking the right as positive, calculate the momentum of each trolley before the collision. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Calculate the velocity of the combined trolleys after the collision, giving its direction. *[3 marks]*

(iii) Calculate the kinetic energy lost and say whether the collision is elastic. *[3 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Momentum is a vector: give opposite directions opposite signs. Conservation of momentum: total momentum before $=$ total momentum after. Kinetic energy is not a vector: $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ is always positive.

### Solution

(i) $p_P = 3 \times 4 = +12\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$ and $p_Q = 2 \times (-3) = -6\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

(ii) Total momentum $= 12 - 6 = 6\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. After the collision: $(3 + 2)\,v = 6 \Rightarrow v = 1.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, positive, so the trolleys move **to the right**.

(iii) Before: $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 4^{2} + \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 3^{2} = 24 + 9 = 33\,\mathrm{J}$.

After: $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 1.2^{2} = 3.6\,\mathrm{J}$.

Kinetic energy lost $= 33 - 3.6 = 29.4\,\mathrm{J}$. Since kinetic energy is not conserved, the collision is **inelastic**: the lost energy is changed into heat, sound and deformation.

enonce_markdown:
A rubber ball of mass $0.4\,\mathrm{kg}$ hits a vertical wall horizontally at $12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and rebounds along the same line at $8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The ball is in contact with the wall for $0.02\,\mathrm{s}$.

(i) Calculate the change in momentum of the ball. *[3 marks]*

(ii) Calculate the average force exerted by the wall on the ball. *[2 marks]*

(iii) State the size and direction of the average force exerted by the ball on the wall, and name the law that justifies your answer. *[2 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The force on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum, $F = \dfrac{mv - mu}{t}$. Velocity is a vector: a rebound reverses the sign of the velocity, so the two speeds add up in the change of momentum.

### Solution

(i) Take the direction towards the wall as positive. Initial momentum: $0.4 \times 12 = +4.8\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. Final momentum: $0.4 \times (-8) = -3.2\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

Change in momentum $= -3.2 - 4.8 = -8.0\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, i.e. a change of size $8.0\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$ away from the wall. (Subtracting the speeds, $12 - 8$, would be wrong.)

(ii) $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{t} = \dfrac{8.0}{0.02} = 400\,\mathrm{N}$, directed away from the wall.

(iii) By Newton's third law, the ball exerts on the wall a force of the same size, $400\,\mathrm{N}$, in the opposite direction, i.e. towards the wall.
